name: Possession of a Penalty Group 1 or 1-B controlled substance (200 to under 400 grams)
officialTitle: OFFENSE: POSSESSION OF SUBSTANCE IN PENALTY GROUP 1 OR 1-B.
conduct: Knowingly or intentionally possessing a substance listed in Penalty Group 1 or 1-B, in an aggregate amount of 200 to under 400 grams, including adulterants and dilutants. Chapter 481 authorizations apply, including obtaining it directly from or under a valid prescription or order of a practitioner acting in professional practice. Possession means actual care, custody, control or management.
penalty: First-degree felony: ordinarily five to 99 years or life and a possible fine up to $10,000. Qualifying felony history may change punishment. A qualifying §481.134(c) drug-free-zone finding increases the minimum prison term by five years and doubles the maximum fine. Punishment increased under §481.134 may not run concurrently with punishment for a conviction under another criminal statute.

name: Possession of dangerous drug (unauthorized possession)
officialTitle: POSSESSION OF DANGEROUS DRUG.
conduct: Possessing a dangerous drug unless it was obtained from a pharmacist or practitioner in the manner §483.042(a)(1) or (2) specifies. Section 483.041(c) excepts listed persons and their agents or employees acting in their usual business, practice or official duties. A limited overdose defense can apply to the first caller who requests emergency medical help for another during an ongoing medical emergency, remains and cooperates, or to the overdose victim when help is requested. Arrest or warrant activity, other offenses outside the statutory exceptions, specified prior dispositions or a request during the preceding 18 months can defeat this defense. A dangerous drug is a device or drug unsafe for self-medication outside the controlled-substance schedules and penalty groups specified in §483.001(2). This charge requires knowing possession or sufficient awareness of control under Penal Code §6.01(b); §6.02 supplies the general rules for culpability.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. Qualifying priors may increase minimum jail time when jail is imposed.

name: Possession of dangerous drug (for purpose of sale)
officialTitle: POSSESSION OF DANGEROUS DRUG.
conduct: Possessing a dangerous drug for the purpose of selling it, except as permitted by Chapter 483. This charge requires knowing possession or sufficient awareness of control under Penal Code §6.01(b); §6.02 supplies the general rules for culpability.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. Qualifying priors may increase minimum jail time when jail is imposed.

name: Possession of marijuana (two ounces or less, qualifying drug-free zone)
officialTitle: OFFENSE: POSSESSION OF MARIHUANA.
conduct: Knowingly or intentionally possessing a usable quantity of marihuana weighing two ounces or less, except as authorized under Chapter 481. The statutory definition excludes hemp. Possession means actual care, custody, control or management. Under §481.121(c) through (e), a limited overdose defense may apply to the first caller who requests emergency help, stays and cooperates, or to the overdose victim. Arrest or warrant activity, other offenses, specified prior outcomes and a request in the preceding 18 months can disqualify a person. Under §481.134(f), the qualifying location must be shown at trial: in, on or within 1,000 feet of the school, school board, youth center or playground property described there; on a school bus; or, for an unauthorized person age 18 or older, in, on or within 1,000 feet of the specified residential-treatment property. Section 481.134(g) excludes an offense inside a private residence when no minor was present.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor on a qualifying zone finding: up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. A qualifying prior may increase minimum jail time if jail is imposed. Enhanced punishment may not run concurrently with punishment for a conviction under another criminal statute.

name: Criminal trespass (general residential operation operating as a residential treatment center)
officialTitle: CRIMINAL TRESPASS.
conduct: Entering or remaining on or in someone else’s property without effective consent after notice that entry was forbidden, or receiving notice to depart and failing to do so. Entry requires the entire body. Notice can include communication from the owner or someone with apparent authority, qualifying fencing or signs, or markings and other conditions specified in §30.05(b). The statute provides exceptions and defenses for particular circumstances, including certain authorized work and firearm-related conduct. The offense must occur on the property of or within a general residential operation actually operating as a residential treatment center. Under Human Resources Code §42.002(4), a general residential operation provides care for seven or more children, 24 hours a day. Other residential programs do not qualify merely because they provide overnight care.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. This is the specified-location grade. If a weapon prohibition is the sole reason entry was forbidden, (d-3) instead ordinarily caps the Class C fine at $200. It provides a Class A exception when, after entry, the person receives the required personal notice and then fails to depart. The separately stated (d)(4) predicate has its own grading rule. Qualifying priors can affect minimum jail time. A qualifying declared disaster or evacuation area can raise the minimum jail term to 180 days.
